input.question: why people think that being in cold weather or swimming in cold water can make you sick
input.ground_truth: Because it can. Moving from extreme temperatures one to another can weaken your immune system and that makes it easier for you to get sick. So while it won't directly make you sick to be out in the cold, going between temps is what will do it. Unless it's something like hypothermia. That can make you sick just from being out in the cold.

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have a little invisible army inside you called "your body's soldiers." Their job is to keep you healthy and fight off germs that can make you sick.

Now, when you are cold—like when it's chilly outside or you swim in cold water—your body has to work a little harder to stay warm. But being cold by itself doesn't put germs inside you. 

Some people think that if you get too cold, the "body soldiers" get sleepy or go away, and then germs can make you sick more easily. But really, it’s not the cold that makes you sick—it’s usually germs that were already around. When you are cold, you might stay inside more, or touch doorknobs that other sick people touched, so you might catch those germs more easily.

So, being cold doesn’t give you a cold or make you sick by magic. It’s usually the germs that do it, but being cold can sometimes help those germs find you!
